topic: SC: a grandson has no right by birth in the share his father got when the grandfather's property was partitioned among Class I heirs - under Section 8, Hindu Succession Act, 1956 the father takes it as his own exclusive property (not coparcenary/HUF property) and could sell it; Section 6 not attracted; Chander Sen and Yudhishter followed; minor's partition suit fails, Madras HC upheld (J. Rajesh (Minor) v. M. Kumaran (Dead) through LRs, C.A. 7020/2012, 2026 INSC 1208, 2026 LiveLaw (SC) 1148, Justices Sunita Agarwal and Augustine George Masih, 6 Nov 2026)

slides.title: No **birthright** for the grandson
slides.subtitle: A share the father got when the grandfather's property was partitioned is the **father's own**. His son cannot claim half of it by birth.
slides.cite: **J. Rajesh (Minor) v. M. Kumaran (Dead) through LRs** · C.A. 7020/2012 · 2026 INSC 1208 · Justices Sunita Agarwal and Augustine George Masih · 6 Nov 2026

slides.label: What happened
slides.title: A son sued over a **sold plot**
bullets: After the grandfather's death, his property in Chennai was divided among his heirs by a **compromise decree in 1994**. The father got a share of **1,811 sq. ft.**
In **1997**, the father sold that share to buyers.
His minor son, born in January 1994, sued through his mother for a **half share**, saying he had a right in it **by birth**.

slides.label: What the Court held
slides.title: Father's share is **his own**
bullets: Under **Section 8** of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, property goes to the **Class I heirs**. A son's son is **not** a Class I heir of his grandfather.
The father takes his share in his **individual capacity**, not as joint family (HUF) property for his own son.
After the partition, each heir's share became that heir's **exclusive property**, which he could sell.

slides.label: The result
slides.title: Grandson's **suit fails**
bullets: The Court said **Section 6** (coparcenary) did not apply, because the son was **not born** when the grandfather died.
It followed its earlier rulings in **Chander Sen (1986)** and **Yudhishter (1987)**.
The appeal was **dismissed**. The Madras High Court's 2010 ruling against the son stands.

slides.label: Keep in mind
slides.title: This is **not** the full picture
bullets: The ruling does **not** say grandsons can never have rights in family property. The answer depends on **how** the property came to the father.
A son can still be an heir to his **father's** property later, under the law of succession.
This post is for information only, not legal advice.

caption:
Is your grandfather's property automatically yours by birth? The Supreme Court says not always 🏠⚖️

After a grandfather's death, his property in Chennai was divided among his heirs by a compromise decree in 1994, and the father got a share of 1,811 sq. ft. In 1997 the father sold it. His minor son, born in January 1994, filed a suit through his mother claiming a half share, saying he had a right in that property by birth.

The Supreme Court disagreed. Under Section 8 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956, the property passes to the Class I heirs, and a son's son is not a Class I heir of his grandfather. The father took his share in his own individual capacity, not as joint family property for his son. Once the property was partitioned, each heir's share became that heir's exclusive property, which he was free to sell. Section 6 did not help, because the son was not born when the grandfather died. The Court followed its earlier rulings in Chander Sen (1986) and Yudhishter (1987) and dismissed the appeal.

Keep in mind: this does not mean grandsons can never have rights in family property. The answer depends on how the property came to the father. Before buying, selling or claiming family property, have the title documents checked properly.

Case: J. Rajesh (Minor) v. M. Kumaran (Dead) through LRs, Civil Appeal No. 7020 of 2012, 2026 INSC 1208
Bench: Justices Sunita Agarwal and Augustine George Masih, Supreme Court, 6 Nov 2026
